items.followUp: Explain how the shape of an enzyme’s active site determines which substrate it can act on.

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme specificity by the matching shapes of the active site and substrate.
rubric.description: States that a substrate with a complementary shape fits the enzyme’s active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the specific fit between the substrate and active site.

rubric.why: The substrate forms a complex with the enzyme, products are released, and the enzyme remains available for reuse.
rubric.description: Describes product formation and states that the enzyme remains unchanged or can be reused.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the product-formation step and the enzyme’s unchanged or reusable state.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, an enzyme’s active site has a specific shape complementary to its substrate, which fits into it like a key into a lock.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released, and the enzyme remains unchanged and can be reused.

items.followUp: State one characteristic of each kingdom in the five-kingdom classification.

rubric.why: Monera have prokaryotic cells, whereas Protista are eukaryotic and mostly unicellular.
rubric.description: Gives a characteristic of Monera and a distinguishing characteristic of Protista.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Monera and 1 mark for Protista; both must be correctly identified.

rubric.why: Fungi obtain food heterotrophically, whereas plants are autotrophs that make food by photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Contrasts the mode of nutrition in Fungi and Plantae.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct characteristic of Fungi and 1 mark for a correct characteristic of Plantae.

rubric.why: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs and are usually capable of movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct characteristic of animals.

modelAnswer: Monera: Organisms are unicellular and prokaryotic; their cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
Protista: Organisms are eukaryotic and mostly unicellular; they may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
Fungi: Organisms are eukaryotic and mostly multicellular, have cell walls, and obtain food heterotrophically by absorption.
Plantae: Organisms are multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls; they are autotrophic and make food by photosynthesis.
Animalia: Organisms are multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; they are heterotrophic and usually capable of movement.
